dossier_statement: Take $n \ge 2$ known and both shapes free. If every count is 0 or $n$, no MLE exists: the likelihood is maximised in the limit by a two-point law on 0 and $n$ when both values occur, and by a point mass when only one does. Otherwise the binomial is the only possible escape. Strict overdispersion, $S^2 > n\hat p(1-\hat p)$ with $\hat p = \bar x/n$ and $S^2$ the sample variance with the number of observations as divisor, is necessary and sufficient for $n \ge 2$ when at least one count is interior. Holding one shape leaves only the point-mass case. With $n = 1$ the shapes are not identified, because the model is a Bernoulli distribution. At $n=0$ both shapes are also unidentified. At known sizes two through eight with an interior count and positive dispersion sign, the attained two-shape fit is unique. With beta held and size free, constant positive data have only a point-mass supremum; all-zero data attain likelihood one at size zero with alpha unidentified. For other samples a finite maximum exists, though the numerical search may stop without resolving it. With alpha held and size free, constant positive data have a point-mass supremum and all-zero data attain likelihood one at size zero with beta unidentified. Other samples may remain unresolved against the negative-binomial face or the size budget.

dossier_statement: For a nonempty sample of nonnegative integer counts with positive mean, a finite MLE with both $n$ and $p$ free exists exactly when $\bar x>v$, where $v=m^{-1}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2$ and $m$ is sample size. All-zero data also attain a maximum, but do not identify the parameters. With probability held, integer maximizers need not be unique. Joint positive-mean multiplicity remains open. With $n>0$ held at an integer at least $\max_i x_i$, $\hat p=\bar x/n$ is unique. Holding $n=0$ requires all-zero data and leaves $p$ unidentified. With $0<p<1$ held, a finite integer maximum exists, possibly at two adjacent sizes. Holding $p=0$ requires all-zero data and leaves $n$ unidentified. Holding $p=1$ requires constant counts and fixes $n$ to that count. With both coefficients held, the observations must have positive probability under the supplied model.

dossier_statement: With all coefficients free, constant positive data have unbounded likelihood. For nonconstant data, a finite MLE exists if and only if some finite point reaches the larger of the optimized Pareto and Weibull log likelihoods (equality is included). These are the only likelihood-retaining escape faces. At least half the sample at its minimum precludes a finite MLE. General joint uniqueness is not established; a successful certificate proves uniqueness for that sample. Numerical finite/face overlap leaves a successful finite search uncertified. With only scale $s$ held, a unique finite maximum exists for nonconstant data if some observation is below $s$. Constant data below $s$ have unbounded likelihood. If all observations are at least $s$, the supremum is on the Pareto path, except that all observations equal to $s$ give unbounded likelihood. Holding $k$ gives a unique finite fit for nonconstant data, but constant data remain unbounded when $c$ and $s$ are free. Holding $c$ reduces existence to the Lomax criterion on $x_i^{c}$, with a possible Weibull limit. Holding both shapes gives a unique scale estimate for any positive sample. Holding $k$ and $s$ gives a unique finite $c$ estimate unless all observations equal $s$. Holding $c$ and $s$ gives a unique finite $k$ estimate. Holding all coefficients leaves likelihood evaluation.

u$ free, constant samples attain likelihood one. Observations on zero and one attain the Bernoulli maximum, which also equals the adjacent CMP limiting supremum. u$ and positive $n$ held, the free probability has a unique mean-matching maximum, including endpoint probabilities. With $p,
u$ held, a feasible free-size maximum is attained when $0<p<1$: for positive dispersion the fixed odds force mass away from bounded counts as $n$ grows, and for negative dispersion the normalizer's endpoint terms bound the tail. With only scale $s$ held, a unique finite maximum exists for nonconstant data if some observation is above $s$. Constant data above $s$ have unbounded likelihood. If all observations are at most $s$, the supremum is on the power path, except that all observations equal to $s$ give unbounded likelihood. Holding $k$ gives a unique finite fit for nonconstant data, but constant data remain unbounded when $c$ and $s$ are free. Holding $c$ reduces existence to the Lomax criterion on $x_i^{-c}$, with a possible inverse Weibull limit. Holding both shapes gives a unique scale estimate for any positive sample. Holding $k$ and $s$ gives a unique finite $c$ estimate unless all observations equal $s$. Holding $c$ and $s$ gives a unique finite $k$ estimate. Holding all coefficients leaves likelihood evaluation.

u$ is free. With $\mu$ and both shapes held, a positive scale maximum exists when $
u(n-k)>k$, where $k$ counts observations at that location; the reverse strict inequality gives unbounded likelihood, and equality is an unattained finite supremum at $\xi=1$ and remains numerically unresolved otherwise. dossier_statement:
With all coefficients free, scale collapse or a skew-normal, half-t, half-normal or two-piece $t_2$ limit can prevent a finite maximum. Global uniqueness is unknown, and the implementation does not certify the full search. The uniform closure theorem exhausts joint escapes in the strict tie regime $3k_{max}<2n$, but its quantitative face profilers are not implemented. Holding coefficients restricts the reachable faces by their moment constraints. Holding $
u$ removes shape escapes, holding $\xi$ removes skew escapes, and holding $\sigma$ excludes a finite-scale $t_2$ face but does not exclude collapse when $
u$ is free. With $\mu$ and both shapes held, a positive scale maximum exists when $
u(n-k)>k$, where $k$ counts observations at that location; the reverse strict inequality gives unbounded likelihood, and equality is an unattained finite supremum at $\xi=1$ and remains numerically unresolved otherwise. With $\sigma$ and both shapes held, a location maximum exists even with ties. Holding all coefficients leaves likelihood evaluation.

With all coefficients free, scale collapse or a skew-normal, half-t, half-normal or two-piece $t_2$ limit can prevent a finite maximum. Global uniqueness is unknown, and the implementation does not certify the full search. The uniform closure theorem exhausts joint escapes in the strict tie regime $3k_{max}<2n$, but its quantitative face profilers are not implemented. Holding coefficients restricts the reachable faces by their moment constraints. Holding $
u$ removes shape escapes, holding $\xi$ removes skew escapes, and holding $\sigma$ excludes a finite-scale $t_2$ face but does not exclude collapse when $
u$ is free. With $\mu$ and both shapes held, a positive scale maximum exists when $
u(n-k)>k$, where $k$ counts observations at that location; the reverse strict inequality gives unbounded likelihood, and equality is an unattained finite supremum at $\xi=1$ and remains numerically unresolved otherwise. With $\sigma$ and both shapes held, a location maximum exists even with ties. Holding all coefficients leaves likelihood evaluation.
